questions.question_text: A 78yearold male patient comes to a psychiatrist with symptoms of depressed mood, low energy, decreased motivation, poor concentration, and decreased appetite. In addition to treating depression, the psychiatrist performs a Mini Mental State Examination. The individual scores 23 out of 30 points. Which of the following statements is Accurate regarding the relationship of depression and major neurocognitive disorders?

options.text: Depression is a predisposing factor for and may be early evidence of major neurocognitive disorder.
Cognitive impairment during depression is irreversible and always progresses to major neurocognitive disorder.
older individuals with cognitive symptoms during depression have the same risk for major neurocognitive disorder as those without cognitive symptoms.
Depression is associated with increased dementia risk only in Parkinson disease.
Depression is linked to increased risk of major neurocognitive disorder only among individuals younger than 75 years.

correct_answer.text: Depression is a predisposing factor for and may be early evidence of major neurocognitive disorder.

questions.explanation: Depression is a risk factor for and may be an early sign of major neurocognitive disorder. Although treatment of depression may improve some associated cognitive symptoms, there is still increased risk of future neurocognitive decline. Elderly patients with cognitive symptoms during a depressive episode are more likely than depressed patients without cognitive symptoms to develop major neurocognitive disorder. Depression is seen in both major vascular neurocognitive disorder and major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer disease and in fact may be more common in the former. Depression has been shown to be a risk factor for major neurocognitive disorder even among the oldest old.

questions.question_text: Which of the following abilities is typically preserved in normal aging?
questions.explanation: Procedural, implicit, and non-declarative memory are typically preserved in normal aging, whereas working memory, processing speed, and fluid intelligence tend to decline.

questions.question_text: Which cognitive function is most consistently resilient in normal aging?
questions.explanation: Working memory is often considered the most consistently resilient cognitive function in normal aging, maintaining relatively stable functionality despite some age-related decline in other domains.

questions.question_text: What percentage of carers of older people with mental health problems will suffer depression at some stage?
questions.explanation: The source directly states 30% of carers will suffer depression at some stage. This is a straightforward factual recall question about carer mental health outcomes. ---

questions.question_text: Many subtypes of vascular dementia have been identifi ed. Which of the following refers to Binswanger’s disease?

options.text: Attenuation of subcortical white matter causing cognitive impairment
Lacunar infarcts in deep brain structures causing cognitive impairment
Cortical surface infarcts causing cognitive impairment
Ventricular enlargement from small vessel disease causing cognitive impairment

correct_answer.text: Attenuation of subcortical white matter causing cognitive impairment

questions.explanation: The term Binswanger’s disease refers to a type of subcortical vascular dementia caused by widespread, microscopic atherosclerotic vascular damage to the deep white matter in the brain. As a result patients may have frontal executive dysfunction, short-term memory loss, and behavioural changes. The most characteristic feature is said to be the reduction of processing speed. An MRI scan of the brain can reveal the characteristic brain lesions essential for diagnosis. Single large infarcts or multiple cortical infarcts give rise to vascular dementia. Periventricular white matter lesions are non-specifi c and are commonly seen in Alzheimer’s dementia, extreme ageing with vascular risk factors, and also in patients with frank vascular dementia. Nagata K, Saito H, Ueno T, et al. Clinical diagnosis of vascular dementia. Journal of the Neurological Sciences 2007; 257: 44–48.

questions.question_text: A 76-year-old man with cataracts presents with visual hallucinations of geometric patterns but denies any delusional content. His cognitive examination is normal. Which diagnosis should be most strongly considered?
questions.explanation: Charles Bonnet syndrome presents specifically with visual hallucinations in the absence of psychotic symptoms (delusions). The source associates it with cataracts (among other visual impairments). The normal cognitive examination and absence of delusions rule out psychotic disorders and dementia. Option E (macular degeneration) is a risk factor for the syndrome, not a diagnosis itself. ---

questions.question_text: Among the following, which statement regarding the assessment of activities of daily living (ADL) in elderly people is correct?

options.text: ADL scales are used as outcome measures
It relies primarily on caregiver observation rather than self-assessment
In dementia, basic ADL decline occurs after instrumental ADL becomes impaired
None of the validated ADL scales depend on the individual’s self-report
The choice of ADL scale in a individual depends on the individual’s gender

correct_answer.text: ADL scales are used as outcome measures

questions.explanation: In dementia complex ADL that require use of tools and equipment (instrumental ADLs) are affected earlier than basic ADL. Although self-report ADL measures are rare, they do exist. For example, the ADL-Prevention Instrument (ADL-PI) has a self-rated version and an informant version. Self-ratings are found to be closer to research observer’s ratings, while family members tend to under-rate the ADL. Data from self-report of functioning predicts mortality better than informant data. The Barthel Index consists of 10 items that measure a person’s ADL and mobility. It can be used to determine a baseline level of functioning and also to monitor changes in ADL over time. It is rated by carers or professionals. Currently, functional capacity measures are being used increasingly in pharmacological trials of patients with dementias as primary outcome measures. ADL scales are not gender biased and are commonly used in both sexes. Massoud F. The role of functional assessment as an outcome measure in antidementia treatment. Can J Neurol Sci 2007; 34 Suppl 1: S47–51.

questions.question_text: Which is the antipsychotic of choice for a 75-year-old man with Parkinson’s disease who presented with psychotic symptoms?
questions.explanation: The American guidelines recommend the use of Clozapine or Quetiapine for the management of psychosis in Parkinson’s disease. The guidelines also note that Olanzapine should not be used for the same. With few exceptions, all atypical antipsychotics have comparable effi cacy against psychosis and the choice is mainly based on their ease of use and the side- effect profi le. Risperidone and olanzapine are associated with sedation. Risperidone can cause considerable worsening of parkinsonism. Olanzapine has been known to worsen cognition and hyperglycaemia in patients with diabetes. A recent Committee on Safety of Medicines warning suggests an increased risk of strokes associated with the use of risperidone and olanzapine in old people. Clozapine has the best evidence for use in Parkinson’s as this was the fi rst atypical antipsychotic that came on the market. However, due to the tedious monitoring protocols, it is seldom used in the population, and it has a restricted licence in the UK. Quetiapine is favoured by many psychiatrists because of its better side-effect profi le and being as effi cacious as Clozapine, at least in one study. Aripiprazole has been shown to worsen Parkinson’s disease. Miyasaki JM, Shannon K, Voon V, et al., Quality Standards Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology. Practice parameter: evaluation and treatment of depression, psychosis, and dementia in Parkinson disease an evidence-based review,: report of the Quality Standards Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology. Neurology 2006; 667: 996–1002. Thanvi BR, Lo TCN and Harsh DP. Psychosis in Parkinson’s disease. Postgraduate Medical Journal 2005; 81: 644–646.

questions.question_text: Suicide is a signifi cant risk when treating elderly individuals with mental health problems. Compared with suicides in younger adults, older individuals who kill themselves are

options.text: More likely to enter into suicide pacts
Less likely to have contact with any healthcare provider in the year before death
More likely to suffer from depression
Less likely to have attempted suicide previously

correct_answer.text: More likely to enter into suicide pacts

questions.explanation: Older patients who commit suicide are more likely to suffer from depressive illness but are less likely to be known to mental health services or to have been treated for depression than younger adults who kill themselves. It is also known that older people are more likely to enter into suicide pacts. In older people, male suicide rates are higher than female suicides. It is generally accepted that the conversion rate of suicidal thoughts to acts is higher in older patients. Murray R, Kendler K, et al., eds. Essential Psychiatry, 4th edn. Cambridge University Press, 2008, p. 374.

questions.question_text: Depression in patients with Parkinson's disease occurs in approximately what percentage?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states Depression occurs in approximately two thirds of patients with PD. This is a direct factual recall from the Parkinson's disease section. ---

questions.question_text: Who theorized that improved control over the id and ego with advanced age gives rise to enhanced self-s ufficiency?
questions.explanation: Freud theorized that heightened control over the id and ego with advanced age leads to more autonomy. Heinz Hartmann was a founder of ego psychology. Erik Erikson is known for his theory of psychosocial development. Bernice Neugarten was a pioneer in the study of aging. Daniel Levinson developed the stagecrisis view of adult development.

questions.question_text: Cholinesterase inhibitors are unlikely to be useful in the clinical approach of

options.text: A diagnosis of lewy body dementia
Vascular dementia with significant white matter disease

questions.explanation: Cholinesterase inhibitors have been shown to be useful in the treatment of senile dementia of Alzheimer’s type, mixed Alzheimer’s and vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, Parkinson’s disease dementia, and young onset Alzheimer’s-type dementia. Too date, there is no evidence of reasonable quality to recommend their use in FTD. Normal levels of cholinacetyltransferase have been demonstrated in patients with FTD compared with reduced levels seen in Alzheimer’s disease; this might explain the lack of effi cacy of cholinesterase inhibitors in FTD. Gelder MG, et al., eds. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 511.

questions.question_text: Auditory impairment in older people has been associated with which psychiatric symptom?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states Auditory impairment has been associated with psychotic symptoms in the elderly. While auditory impairment may be associated with other psychiatric symptoms, psychotic symptoms are specifically identified in the material. ---

questions.question_text: What would be the firstline pharmacological treatment recommendation for late-l ife schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: A 2004 consensus survey of 48 American experts concluded that the firstline recommendation for latelife schizophrenia 204 • PSYCHIATRY is risperidone, 1.25 to 3 mg daily. Olanzapine, quetiapine, and aripiprazole are considered secondline treatment. Re FeRe NCe Alexopoulos GS, Streim J, Carpenter D, Docherty JP (2004). Expert consensus panel for using antipsychotic drugs in older patients: Using antipsychotic agents in older patients. Journal of Clinical Psychiatry, 65, 5– 99.

questions.question_text: What outcome has been associated with volunteering for 100 or more hours per year in older adults?
questions.explanation: Volunteering for 100 hours or more per year is associated with reduced risk of dementia in older adults and more positive self-perceptions of aging, which predict fewer depressive symptoms.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old woman presents to the primary care physician with complaints of difficulty concentrating over the last 4 weeks. “My brain is in a fog. I’m having trouble remembering things as well.” She worries that she is showing signs of Alzheimer dementia, “like my father did before he died.” She states that she used to do crossword puzzles daily to stay sharp, “but now I can’t even finish one, so I’ve lost interest.” She reports difficulty getting to sleep, which she attributes to anxiety about “forgetting things and losing my mind.” She notes that she has lost about 4 pounds over the last month due to decreased appetite. She has no chronic medical illnesses and takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals no abnormalities. Urinalysis, urine drug screen, complete blood count, and comprehensive metabolic panel are all within normal limits. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Given the patient’s relatively sudden and acute onset of cognitive difficulties, it is unlikely that she has Alzheimer dementia, or that this is normal aging, both of which would be much more gradual... Another explanation for her symptoms of poor concentration, loss of interest in crossword puzzles, difficulty sleeping, and decreased appetite is major depressive disorder. If depression profoundly affects cognition in the elderly, it is sometimes referred to as “pseudodementia.”

questions.question_text: Median survival from the time of diagnosis for individuals with Alzheimer’s dementia (AD) is
questions.explanation: It is important to note that AD by itself is not a fatal disease. The median survival time following a diagnosis of AD depends strongly on the patient’s age at diagnosis. The older the age at diagnosis, the higher the chances of death. For example, some studies have shown a difference in median survival time of around 5 years between those diagnosed with dementia at the age of 65 and those diagnosed at the age of 90. The median survival from initial diagnosis is higher for men than women in some studies but this is not consistently shown. The presence of frontal lobe release signs, extrapyramidal signs, and gait disturbance, history of falls, congestive heart failure, ischaemic heart disease, and diabetes at baseline may predict shorter survival. Based on numerous longitudinal studies, a median survival of 5–8 years has been estimated. A multicentre prospective population-based cohort study in England and Wales with 14 years’ follow-up reported median survival after the estimated onset of dementia as 4.6 years for women and 4.1 years for men. There was a difference of nearly 7 years in survival between the younger old and the oldest people with dementia: 10.7 years for ages 65–69 vs. 3.8 years for ages ≥90. Signifi cant factors that predicted mortality in the presence of dementia during the follow-up included sex, age of onset, and disability before the onset. Type of accommodation, marital status, and self-reported health were not associated with survival. Gelder MG et al., eds. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 336. Larson EB, Shadlen M-F, Wang L, et al. Survival after Initial Diagnosis of Alzheimer Disease. Annals of Internal Medicine 2004; 140: 501–509. Xie J, Brayne C, and Matthews FE et al. Survival times in people with dementia: analysis from population based cohort study with 14 year follow up. British Medical Journal 2008; 10: 1136.

questions.question_text: Which key standard was outlined in the National Service Framework for Older People (2001)?

options.text: All older people should be assessed annually for mental health
Older people with mental health problems should have access to specialist services
Primary care should manage all older adult mental health presentations
Mental health services should prioritize dementia assessment over functional illness
Social services should provide all mental health interventions for older adults

correct_answer.text: Older people with mental health problems should have access to specialist services

questions.explanation: The source explicitly identifies this as a key standard from the 2001 National Service Framework. Options A, C, D, and E either misrepresent the framework's emphasis or contradict the guidance about integrated specialist services. ---

questions.question_text: Which is the most commonly used screening tool to diagnose dementia in older people?
questions.explanation: MMSE: Cut off 24/30, takes 5-10 minutes to complete and is a standard baseline test. It is the most widely used cognitive test in old age psychiatry and has been validated in a variety of populations. It is good for screening global cognitive dysfunctions as opposed to focal cognitive dysfunctions. It covers the following areas of cognition such as orientation, memory, concentration, language, praxis and Gnosis

questions.question_text: Among the following, which diagnostic tests has been most widely used to monitor treatment response in anticholinesterase trials for dementia?

options.text: Behaviour Pathology in Alzheimer's Disease rating scale
Alzheimer’s disease assessment scale – cognitive section (ADAS-Cog)

correct_answer.text: Alzheimer’s disease assessment scale – cognitive section (ADAS-Cog)

questions.explanation: The ADAS-Cog is used as the de facto standard primary outcome neuropsychological measure for dementia trials. It measures several cognitive domains, including memory, language, and praxis with total scores ranging from 0 to 70. A four-point change on the ADAS-Cog at 6 months after starting antidementia drugs has been used as an arbitrary cut-off point indicating a clinically important difference. This pharmaceutical cut-off on ADAS-Cog must be interpreted in the context of overall response when it is translated to clinical practice. MMSE is not as sensitive to change as ADAS-Cog; hence, it is rarely used as a primary outcome measure in dementia trials. An MRI brain scan currently has no role in monitoring treatment response. Rockwood K, Fay S, Gorman M, et al. The clinical meaningfulness of ADAS-Cog changes in Alzheimer’s disease patients treated with donepezil in an open-label trial. BMC Neurology 2007; 7: 26.

questions.question_text: In the pharmacological clinical approach of delirium, haloperidol is the preferred agent from the available antipsychotic drugs. All of the following explain the above with the exception of

options.text: Availability of multiple routes of administration for haloperidol
Availability of guided dosing strategies for haloperidol in delirium
Low incidence of extrapyramidal side effects
Minimal interaction with other medications commonly used in elderly

correct_answer.text: Availability of guided dosing strategies for haloperidol in delirium

questions.explanation: Many practice guidelines for the treatment of patients with delirium support the use of antipsychotics as the drugs of choice in delirium. Haloperidol is the most frequently used due to the different available routes of administration, a lack of anticholinergic side-effects, few active metabolites, and the low likelihood of causing adverse effects such as sedation and hypotension, which can be diffi cult to manage in an acute confusional state. But as QT prolongation is a possible side-effect, it is advisable to have a baseline ECG before such use is attempted in high- risk patients. These recommendations do not have much evidence base but are largely driven by retrospective chart surveys; hence, there is a dearth of data on dosage guidance. It is suggested that haloperidol is given at half the adult dose in elderly people. Tyrer P and Silk K., eds. Cambridge Textbook of Effective Treatments in Psychiatry. Cambridge University Press, 2008, p 181.

questions.question_text: In what approximate percentage of people with chronic physical illness does depression occur?
questions.explanation: Depression occurs in around 20% of people suffering from chronic physical illness. This is a straightforward factual recall question. ---

questions.question_text: In the elderly, which of the following occurs with hydrophobic (lipophilic) drugs compared to younger adults?
questions.explanation: Elderly individuals have more body fat and less body water than younger adults, leading to an increased volume of distribution and longer duration of action for lipophilic drugs like diazepam.

questions.question_text: All of the below options apply are linked to a higher risk of elder abuse with the exception of

options.text: Cognitive impairment in the victim increases vulnerability
History of substance abuse in the perpetrator
Perpetrator being financially dependent on the victim

questions.explanation: Various risk factors have been proposed from prospective analysis of elder abuse. Shared living situation is a major risk factor; older people living alone are at lowest risk. Having a ‘poor social network’ and subsequent social isolation signifi cantly increases the risk of mistreatment. A diagnosis of dementia makes elderly people more vulnerable to mistreatment. The prevalence rates of elder abuse in samples of dementia caregivers is far higher than the elder abuse seen in the general community. Similarly, a higher rate of mental illness, such as depression or substance abuse, among caregivers increases the risk of elder abuse. It is also found that perpetrators of elder abuse tend to be fi nancially dependent on the abused individual. Lachs, MS and Pillemer, K. Elder abuse. Lancet 2004; 364: 1263–1273.

questions.question_text: During old age, a person gives up due to socioeconomic reasons. Which theory explains this?
questions.explanation: Social exchange theory explains that age reduces the ability to engage in reciprocal roles, and retirement represents a social contract exchanging productivity for leisure.

questions.question_text: During old age, a person gives up a pressurized career for socio-economic reasons. What is this process called?
questions.explanation: Downshifting refers to voluntary opting out of a pressurized career and giving up a well-paid job for a more fulfilling life. This is distinct from other theories of aging and role change.

questions.question_text: Which theory explains giving and reciprocity by suggesting that aging robs people of the ability to engage in reciprocal roles?
questions.explanation: Social exchange theory suggests that retirement is a special social contract in which productivity is exchanged for increased leisure and decreased responsibilities. It specifically addresses how aging affects the ability to maintain reciprocal social roles and exchange relationships.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is one of the brain areas that is affected very early in Alzheimer‘s disease?
questions.explanation: At first

questions.question_text: A 79-year-old woman with dementia living in a residential home is noted to have become increasingly withdrawn and stopped attending social activities she previously enjoyed. Her carer mentions that the patient's regular medications have been held twice due to pharmacy delays. Considering the role of medication in older people's physical and mental health, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Assume the behavioral change reflects disease progression
Ensure medication regimens and timings are restored and maintained, then reassess

correct_answer.text: Ensure medication regimens and timings are restored and maintained, then reassess

questions.explanation: The source specifically emphasizes that in Parkinson's disease (and by extension, important medication regimens in older people), failure to maintain normal dosing schedules can result in delirium and depression, slowed cognition and anxiety. While this example is from PD, the principle extends to other medication-dependent conditions. The withdrawal and functional decline may be iatrogenic from medication interruption. Ensuring medication continuity and reassessing is the most appropriate intervention before assuming disease progression. This requires linking medication adherence to psychiatric symptoms—a two-step inference. ---

questions.question_text: Lily Flanders is 89 years old and lives in a care home. She has had gradual cognitive impairment for the past decade, and over the past 6 months her behaviour has become more unpredictable: sometimes she can be extremely friendly and over-familiar, at other times she‘s irritable, shouting at the staff. She experiences a fall with minor head injury, and whilst admitted to the ward an MRI of her brain is requested. Which areas of the brain are most likely to be affected in relation to Mrs Flander‘s dementia and behavioural disturbance, as shown by MRI investigation?
questions.explanation: Fronto-temporal region, whose functioning is responsible for cognition and behaviour, is likely to be atrophied in cases of dementia with behavioural disturbance.

questions.question_text: A 72-year-old man with Parkinson's disease has been attending appointments irregularly. His wife reports he has recently become withdrawn, tearful, and has been missing several doses of his medication daily. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate explanation for his current presentation?

options.text: Early-onset dementia related to Parkinson's disease
Development of a new depressive episode
Psychotic relapse due to age-related brain changes

correct_answer.text: Development of a new depressive episode

questions.explanation: The source identifies that depression occurs in approximately two-thirds of Parkinson's disease patients. The clinical presentation (withdrawal, tearfulness) is consistent with depression. Importantly, medication non-adherence in PD is described as a trigger for delirium and depression, slowed cognition and anxiety, suggesting that medication irregularity combined with depressive symptoms points to depression. Option C (delirium) would typically present with acute confusion rather than persistent withdrawal. Option A (dementia in PD) is possible but the current presentation is more consistent with depression, which is more common. ---

questions.question_text: Which cognitive domain is NOT listed as commonly affected in Parkinson's disease?
questions.explanation: The source identifies higher executive dysfunction, attention, memory, visuomotor processing and visual attention as common cognitive deficits in PD. Language production is not mentioned. Option D is the only cognitive domain not explicitly listed in the source material. ---

questions.question_text: Dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, endocrine changes, and infection can produce which type of symptom in older people with acute illness?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states Metabolic changes during illness can accentuate the emotional response to it – dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, endocrine changes and infection can all produce affective symptoms. Affective symptoms refer to mood symptoms. While these conditions may cause other symptom types, affective symptoms are specifically identified here. ---

questions.question_text: Parkinson's Disease with Cognitive Decline A 72-year-old with Parkinson's disease on levodopa and citalopram presents with MMSE 21/30, insomnia, and visual hallucinations. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Rivastigmine is licensed for Parkinson's disease dementia. It improves cognition and may help hallucinations. Avoid typical antipsychotics in PD.

questions.question_text: Which of the following about old age pharmacokinetics is true?

options.text: Absorption is increased compared to younger adults
Free drug concentration in plasma increases

correct_answer.text: Free drug concentration in plasma increases

questions.explanation: In elderly patients, there is increased free drug concentration in plasma due to decreased plasma protein binding and altered distribution, leading to increased drug effects.

questions.question_text: Compared with mania at younger age of onset, late-onset mania in elderly people is distinguished by

options.text: Greater frequency of secondary mania due to medical conditions or medications
Greater risk of chronic mood instability following recovery

questions.explanation: Late-life mania is often different from earlier onset mania. There is a prominent mixture of depressive symptoms in late-life mania; in addition, those with late-onset mania are more likely to have had a depressed phase during their fi rst admission. Occasionally, manic symptoms in late life may herald the onset of frontal-type dementia. It is also shown that men may have higher rates of mania in late-life than women – one series reported a difference of 60% in men to 10% in women. A signifi cant association with cerebral organic disease has been demonstrated, leading to the term secondary mania in cases with organic aetiology. A higher tendency to fi nd vascular lesions in neuroimaging studies of older manic patients has been described. Similar to geriatric depression, late-life mania is also said to have less genetic contribution to aetiology than younger adults with mania. Murray R, Kendler K, et al., eds. Essential Psychiatry, 4th edn. Cambridge University Press, 2008, p. 369.

questions.question_text: According to social exchange theory, what does retirement represent in the context of aging?

options.text: A special social contract exchanging productivity for leisure

correct_answer.text: A special social contract exchanging productivity for leisure

questions.explanation: Social exchange theory proposes that retirement is a special social contract wherein individuals exchange productivity and work responsibilities for increased leisure time and decreased responsibilities. Age reduces the ability to engage in reciprocal roles, and this exchange is socially negotiated.

questions.question_text: EMI: During old age a person give up due to Socio-economic reasons:
questions.explanation: Social exchange theory describes retirement as a social contract wherein productivity is exchanged for increased leisure and decreased responsibilities. In the context of socioeconomic factors forcing older adults to reduce activities, this represents the cost-benefit analysis inherent in social exchange theory.

questions.question_text: An 81-year-old man is assessed in his home following referral from his GP for mood disturbance. During the assessment, his daughter provides crucial information about his premorbid personality and his current functional abilities that would not have been evident in clinic. Which aspect of the home assessment is this illustrating?

options.text: Depth and quality of information obtained through collateral history and observation of functional context
Avoidance of the need for physical examination
Elimination of the need for further investigations

correct_answer.text: Depth and quality of information obtained through collateral history and observation of functional context

questions.explanation: The source identifies depth and quality of information as a key advantage of home assessments, and informant interview is described as particularly important in assessment. The daughter's collateral information and the contextual functional observations represent the quality and depth advantage of home-based assessment. The other options either misrepresent benefits or are not specifically identified in the source. ---

questions.question_text: Memory complaints that do not qualify for a diagnosis of dementia are commonly in elderly people. All of the following are shown to predict conversion from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to dementia with the exception of

options.text: Presence of amnestic subtype of MCI
Objective decline in cognitive test performance over time
Biomarker evidence of amyloid pathology on imaging

questions.explanation: The presence of hippocampal atrophy in patients with amnestic MCI may predict the onset of later dementia. The risk of conversion to dementia is four times higher in 5 years when hippocampal atrophy is present. It is generally accepted that the closer one’s cognitive ability, brain imaging, and genetic susceptibility are to AD, the more likely is the progression to dementia from MCI. Other factors predicting conversion include older age, greater severity of baseline cognitive defi cits, especially impaired episodic recall and hypoperfusion of multiple brain regions in neuroimaging studies. It is also noted that multidomain amnestic MCI has a higher conversion rate than pure amnestic MCI. This conversion is more pronounced if the cognitive complaints are accompanied by carers’ reports of impaired daily function. Sensory impairment has no role in such predictions. DeCarli C. Mild cognitive impairment: prevalence, prognosis, aetiology, and treatment. Lancet Neurology 2003; 2: 15–21.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which prevents or delays major neurocognitive disorder?

options.text: Adequate blood pressure and diabetes management
Cognitive training and mental stimulation in early dementia
Prevention of craniocerebral traumas earlier in life and control of vascular disease

correct_answer.text: Prevention of craniocerebral traumas earlier in life and control of vascular disease

questions.explanation: The prevention of craniocerebral traumas earlier in life through highway speed limits, use of crash helmets and

questions.question_text: A 72-year-old man exhibits paranoid delusions and ideas of reference. The most commonly cause of new onset psychotic symptoms in this age group is

options.text: A diagnosis of very late-onset schizophrenia
A diagnosis of lewy body dementia

questions.explanation: Psychosis is a prominent non-cognitive symptom seen in Alzheimer’s dementia. The prevalence of psychosis in patients with Alzheimer’s dementia has been estimated at 30–50%. Psychotic symptoms are seen in 0.2–4.7% of the elderly population in the community. In nursing homes the prevalence rates are very high – 10–60%. Dementia accounts for the highest number of psychotic symptoms diagnosed among elderly people. Prospective studies have shown that 36.7% of patients with psychotic symptoms may have dementia, most likely of Alzheimer’s type. Holroyd S and Laurie S. Correlates of psychotic symptoms among elderly outpatients. International Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry 1999; 14: 379–384.

questions.question_text: Which ability is typically preserved in normal aging?
questions.explanation: Procedural, implicit, and non-declarative memory are preserved in normal aging, along with spatial abilities. Declarative and working memory tend to decline with normal aging.

questions.question_text: What does the source identify as the key advantage of undertaking new psychiatric assessments at a patient's home rather than in clinic?

options.text: Depth and quality of information obtained, and avoidance of tiring and expensive journeys
Easier access to physical examination equipment

correct_answer.text: Depth and quality of information obtained, and avoidance of tiring and expensive journeys

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states There are many advantages to undertaking new assessments at the patient's home, particularly for people with dementia – depth and quality of information, and avoidance of a potentially tiring and expensive journey for patients. This is a direct factual statement about assessment location. ---

questions.question_text: Based on Bernice Neugarten, the primary conflict of old age involves:

options.text: Coping with loss of independence and medical decline
Management of chronic pain and physical limitations

questions.explanation: Bernice Neugarten dedicated much of her life’s work to the subject of adult development and the psychology of aging. She believed that the primary conflict of old age involved relinquishing authority and assessing accomplishments. Kohut believed the major task of old age was preservation of self-e steem.

questions.question_text: The post-stroke incidence of stroke related to antipsychotic use is approximately:
questions.explanation: Antipsychotics are associated with an approximately 1% increased risk of stroke; this risk is higher in elderly patients and with typical antipsychotics.

questions.question_text: A patient with mild cognitive impairment wants to know how to reduce dementia risk. Which intervention is most evidence-supported?
questions.explanation: Smoking cessation is a modifiable risk factor with strong evidence for reducing dementia risk; aspirin use has limited evidence and is comorbidity-dependent.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old man with newly diagnosed early Parkinson's disease is referred to your clinic. Which aspect of his management is described as very important in the source material?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states Medication regimens and timings are very important – failure to maintain normal dosing schedules can result in delirium and depression, slowed cognition and anxiety in Parkinson's disease. This highlights a critical management principle specific to PD. The other options, while potentially relevant, are not specifically identified as very important in the source material. ---

questions.question_text: The Hachinski Ischaemic Score is used to aid clinical differentiation of Alzheimer’s dementia from vascular dementia. Which of the following clinical features support a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s dementia rather than vascular dementia?
questions.explanation: The Hachinski Ischaemic Score is an easy-to-use clinical tool that aids in the bedside differentiation of Alzheimer’s dementia from vascular dementia. It has been validated in patients with pathologically confi rmed dementia. A cut-off score ≤4 supports a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s dementia while a score ≥7 favours vascular dementia. These cut-off values have a sensitivity of 89% and a specifi city of 89%. Abrupt onset, fl uctuating course, history of stroke, presence of focal neurological symptoms and signs strongly favour a diagnosis of vascular dementia. Other supporting features for a diagnosis of vascular dementia include stepwise deterioration, presence of nocturnal confusion, absence of changes in personality, presence of emotional incontinence, depression and a history of hypertension. Moroney JT. Meta-analysis of the Hachinski Ischaemic Score in pathologically verifi ed dementias. Neurology 1997; 49: 1096–1105.

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old woman in an assisted living facility becomes irritable several evenings a week about an hour after dinner, and questions where she is and how she got there. She has a standing order of as-needed quetiapine, which settles her and helps her sleep through the night. When she wakes in the morning, she is alert and oriented to person, place, and time, socializes easily with the staff and friends she has made, and does not recall much of her behavior from the night before. What neurotransmitter most likely plays the primary role in the patient’s evening behaviors?
questions.explanation: Sundowning is a type of delirium that occurs usually in elderly who have a diagnosis of dementia. The phenomenon is marked by confusion and behavioral changes. Though symptoms are often mitigated with an antipsychotic, which acts primarily on dopamine and, in some medications, serotonin, the primary neurotransmitter involved in delirium is thought to be acetylcholine.

questions.question_text: According to the JCPMH guidance, services for older people's mental health must be interdisciplinary. What does this encompass?

options.text: All relevant disciplines involved in assessment and management

correct_answer.text: All relevant disciplines involved in assessment and management

questions.explanation: Older people's mental health services must be disciplinary (likely meaning multidisciplinary). The context and the integration guidelines emphasize that services must involve close working with social services, primary care, community services, voluntary services and geriatricians, indicating an all-encompassing interdisciplinary approach. Option A is too restrictive, and options C, D, and E exclude relevant disciplines mentioned in the source. ---

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is a predictor of longterm care placement of persons with neurocognitive disorder?

options.text: Primary caregiver living in the home
Behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia

correct_answer.text: Behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia

questions.explanation: Behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia increase the risk of long-term care placement, as do white race, older age, dementia severity, caregiver burden, and greater functional impairment.

questions.question_text: The most effective psychological clinical measure to reduce depression and emotional burden in caregivers of people with dementia is
questions.explanation: A systematic review of studies looking at improvements in caregiver psychological health revealed that six or more sessions of individual behavioural management therapy had the highest quality of evidence. This intervention was effective for up to 32 months after intervention. There was some evidence supporting individual and group caregiver coping sessions to reduce depression among caregivers; the benefi ts may last up to 3 months. Educational interventions, group behavioural management sessions, fewer than six individual behavioural management sessions, and supportive therapy were not effective interventions for reducing a caregiver’s symptoms. Selwood A, Johnston K, Katona C, et al. Systematic review of the effect of psychological interventions on family caregivers of people with dementia. Journal of Affective Disorders 2007; 101: 75–89.

questions.question_text: In elderly patients over 80 years old, kidney function declines by approximately:
questions.explanation: In patients above age 80, approximately 15% of kidney function is lost, affecting drug clearance and requiring dose adjustments.

questions.question_text: In CJD pathological study of brain tissue shows spongiosis with neuronal loss, gliosis, and amyloid plaques. These amyloid plaques contain
questions.explanation: The core neuropathology of CJD is characterized by spongiform change, neuronal loss, astrocytosis, and amyloid plaque formation. The amyloid plaques in CJD are generally made of insoluble prion proteins. In addition, abnormal neuritic dendrites with white matter necrosis and beta protein amyloid angiopathy may also be seen. Tetsuyuki KJT, Takatoshi T, Takeshita I, et al. Amyloid plaques in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease stain with prion protein antibodies. Annals of Neurology 1986; 20: 204–208.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which methods of psychological clinical approach of neuropsychiatric symptoms of dementia uses materials such as old newspapers and household items to stimulate memories and enable people to share and value their experiences?
questions.explanation: Reminiscence therapy uses materials such as old newspapers and household items to stimulate memories and enable people to share and value their experiences. The evidence base for this therapy in improving behavioural problems is limited. It may have a modest impact on mood symptoms. Validation therapy is based on Rogerian humanistic psychology; it encourages individual uniqueness and gives the opportunity to resolve confl icts by encouraging and validating the expression of feelings and emotions. Reality orientation therapy is based on the fact that patients with dementia function poorly secondary to impairment in orientating information (day, date, weather, time, and use of names) Hence reminders can improve functioning. Cognitive stimulation therapy is similar to reality orientation therapy but aims at improving information processing rather than factual knowledge to address problems in functioning in patients with dementia. Snoezelen therapy is also called multisensory stimulation. It is grounded on the supposition that neuropsychiatric symptoms may result from periods of sensory deprivation. It combines relaxation and exploration of sensory stimuli (e.g. lights, sounds, and tactile sensations). Livingston G, Johnston K, Katona C, et al. Systematic review of psychological approaches to the management of neuropsychiatric symptoms of dementia. American Journal of Psychiatry 2005; 162: 1996–2021.

questions.question_text: Assessment of activities of daily living in Alzheimer's disease:
questions.explanation: MOHOST (Model of Human Occupation Screening Tool) is the primary assessment tool for activities of daily living endorsed for use in evaluating functional abilities in Alzheimer's disease.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which scales can be used to record the behavioural and psychological features linked to dementia in elderly people?
questions.explanation: The Neuropsychiatric inventory (NPI) can be used to measure behavioural and psychological features of dementia in elderly people. It was created by Cummings et al. It evaluates 10–12 neuropsychiatric disturbances common to dementia using frequency, severity and the carer’s distress as indices. The Bristol scale is used to measure activities of daily living; the Cornell depression scale is used to assess depression in demented patients. The abbreviated mental test is a quick and easily administered test that is used as a screening tool for dementia. Kaufer DI, Cummings JL, Ketchel P, et al. Validation of the NPI-Q, a brief clinical form of the Neuropsychiatric Inventory. Journal of Neuropsychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences 2000; 12: 233–9.

questions.question_text: An 80-year-old woman with eGFR >25 ml/min requires an antipsychotic. Which would be most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Amisulpride is preferred in renal impairment as it has minimal hepatic metabolism and can be safely used with eGFR >30; others require more dose adjustment.

questions.question_text: An 88-year-old woman is admitted to hospital following a stroke affecting her right hemisphere. On day 5 of admission, nursing staff report she is crying uncontrollably at minor frustrations despite reporting feeling well. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Pathological crying and emotional lability are specifically described in the source as relatively common post stroke and distinct from true depression or adjustment disorder. The timing (day 5) and the discrepancy between mood report and behavior fit this presentation. Options A and B would typically involve subjective mood changes, which this patient denies. ---

questions.question_text: A patient with mild cognitive impairment asks about prognosis. What percentage of people with MCI convert to dementia within 1 year?
questions.explanation: Approximately 10% of MCI cases progress to dementia per year.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is not considered among the primary psychosocial factors contributing to the increased risk for suicide among older adults?

options.text: A diagnosis of advancing medical illness

questions.explanation: The elderly have a higher risk for suicide compared with the general population. Older adults cite loneliness, financial problems, medical illness, depression, and loss as reasons for suicidal ideation. Although access to 1. dEvElOPmENT THROu potentially lethal medications such as opioids is common among older adults, access itself does not increase the risk of suicidal thoughts. Geriatric patients should be routinely evaluated for depression and suicidality.

questions.question_text: An 80-year-old woman with Alzheimer's dementia develops low mood and is started on an antidepressant. Two weeks later, she presents with spontaneous bruising and a nosebleed. Which class of antidepressant is most likely responsible for the increased bleeding risk?
questions.explanation: SSRIs impair platelet function; combined with anticoagulants significantly increases bleeding risk.

questions.question_text: A 67-year-old retired educational psychologist exhibits forgetfulness. All of the following are features seen in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) with the exception of

options.text: Objective cognitive impairment on neuropsychological testing
Preserved ability to perform complex problem-solving tasks
Absence of dementia syndrome and functional decline
Presence of family history of dementia

correct_answer.text: Presence of family history of dementia

questions.explanation: An array of various terms has been used to describe age-associated cognitive impairment not amounting to dementia. The most popular term is MCI, of which several types have been described of late. The amnestic MCI refers to the original description of MCI. Diagnosis of MCI requires the presence of memory complaint (preferably corroborated by an informant), objective memory impairment for age, preserved general cognitive function, normal functional activities, and no dementia. The presence or absence of family history of dementia is not a criterion used to describe MCI. Chong MS, and Sahadevan S. Preclinical Alzheimer’s disease: diagnosis and prediction of progression. Lancet Neurology 2005; 4: 576–579.

questions.question_text: All of the below options apply are necessary to establish the competence to make a will with the exception of

options.text: The person should understand the significance of making a will
The person should have a broad understanding of the extent of his/her estate
The person should be aware of the natural heirs and dependents
The person should not have a disorder affecting his/her mind
The person should act of his/her own free volition

correct_answer.text: The person should not have a disorder affecting his/her mind

questions.explanation: Testamentary capacity refers to the competence for drafting and signing a will. In English law, this is based on case Banks v Goodfellow in 1870. The capacity to draw a will requires 1. understanding the nature of the act of drawing a will and its effects 2. understanding the extent of the property being disposed 3. understanding the nature and extent of the claims of those who are included or excluded in the will 4. absence of mental disorder that can affect the previous (1–3) competencies 5. absence of undue infl uence (duress) by third parties. Hence a mentally ill individual can have full testamentary capacity if his/her mental illness does not directly infl uence his/her understanding of the process, the extent of his/her estate, or the nature of claims that could be made to his/her estate. Murray B and Jacoby R. The interface between old age psychiatry and the law. Advances in Psychiatric Treatment 2002; 8: 271–278.

questions.question_text: Which of the following sensory impairments is most commonly associated with Charles Bonnet syndrome?
questions.explanation: Charles Bonnet syndrome is most commonly associated with macular degeneration and also mentions association with cataracts and diabetic retinopathy. Macular degeneration is identified as the primary association. ---

questions.question_text: What is the most common medication used for treating patients with Lewy body dementia and psychosis?
questions.explanation: Cholinesterase inhibitors, particularly rivastigmine, are first-line management for cognitive impairment, psychosis, and agitation in Lewy body dementia. Rivastigmine has been shown to alleviate visual hallucinations, delusions, anxiety, and apathy in DLB with lower risk of neuroleptic sensitivity compared to antipsychotics.

questions.question_text: Which is the most common cause of disability among adults 65 years and older?
questions.explanation: Only arthritis is a more common cause of disability among those aged 65 years and older than dementia. Dementia increases with age, with about 20% having severe dementia by 80 years old.

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states the proportion will double from about 11% to 22% between 2000 and 2050. This is a straightforward factual recall question about global demographic projections. ---

questions.question_text: What function is preserved in normal aging?
questions.explanation: Spatial abilities tend to be relatively preserved during normal aging, whereas working memory, processing speed, and episodic memory typically decline with age.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is an observational tool designed to evaluate the quality of care and well-being of people with dementia in formal care settings?

options.text: A diagnosis of dementia Care Mapping (DCM)

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of dementia Care Mapping (DCM)

questions.explanation: DCM is an observational tool designed to evaluate the quality of care and well-being of people with dementia in formal care settings. It was designed by Kitwood in 1992. DCM is based on the social–psychological theory of dementia care, which states that much of the decline in patients with dementia is a direct consequence of the social and environmental situation experienced. Better social care may result in less suffering than would otherwise be expected from their neurological state. The Washington University CDR is a global scale developed to clinically denote the presence of Alzheimer’s dementia and stage its clinical severity using semi-structured interviews with the patient and informants. The Burden Interview and Caregiver Burden Scale are used to measure the degree of caregiver strain. Beavis D, Simpson S, and Graham I. A literature review of dementia care mapping: methodological considerations and effi cacy. Journal of Psychiatric and Mental Health Nursing 2002; 9: 725–736.

questions.question_text: An 80-year-old woman recently started on donepezil presents with ankle swelling. The most appropriate management is:
questions.explanation: Ankle swelling/peripheral edema is a known side effect of donepezil that may resolve with dose reduction; this is the most conservative initial approach.

questions.question_text: What cognitive outcome is associated with volunteering for 100 or more hours per year in older adults?
questions.explanation: Volunteering for 100 hours or more per year is associated with older adults having more positive self-perceptions of aging and fewer depressive symptoms, which subsequently predicts reduced dementia risk.

questions.question_text: Schizophrenia-like psychosis is a prominent feature of which of the following dementing illnesses?

options.text: A diagnosis of lewy body dementia

questions.explanation: Huntington’s disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. It is a neurodegenerative disorder related to expansion of a trinucleotide repeat sequence in the short arm of chromosome 4. Clinical features include a triad of choreic movements, cognitive decline, and psychiatric syndromes starting in the fourth to fi fth decade. Psychiatric presentation is usually variable and can precede motor and cognitive changes. Most common psychiatric problems include change in personality (impulsive, disinhibited, and dissocial) and depression. Paranoid schizophrenia-like symptoms occur in 6–25% of cases. Such schizophrenia-like presentation is very rare in other conditions listed. Correa B, Xavier M, and Guimaraes J. Association of Huntington’s disease and schizophrenia-like psychosis in a Huntington’s disease pedigree. Clinical Practice and Epidemiology in Mental Health 2006; 2: 1.

questions.question_text: Aggressive Alzheimer's Patient A patient with Alzheimer's disease shows persistent aggression despite behavioral interventions and environmental modifications. Which antipsychotic has the best evidence for aggression in dementia?
questions.explanation: Risperidone is the only antipsychotic licensed (in UK) for short-term treatment of persistent aggression in Alzheimer's disease.

questions.question_text: Which cognitive function is most consistently resilient in normal ageing?
questions.explanation: Working memory is often considered the most consistently resilient cognitive function in normal aging, maintaining relatively good functionality compared to other domains like selective attention and spatial orientation, although processing speed declines with age.

questions.question_text: Which memory type is preserved in normal aging?

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is not considered an significant predictor for successful aging?
questions.explanation: Predictors for successful aging include higher education level, absence of alcohol abuse and cigarette smoking, absence of depression, maintenance of appropriate weight, regular exercise, and social supports. However, social class does not appear to be an important predictor for successful aging.

questions.question_text: The greatest risk factor for vascular dementia is:
questions.explanation: The greatest risk factors for stroke, white matter hyperintensities, and consequently vascular dementia are high systolic and high diastolic blood pressure. Hypertension is the most significant modifiable risk factor for vascular dementia, as it directly damages cerebral blood vessels and increases stroke risk, leading to vascular cognitive impairment.

questions.question_text: A 68-year-old man with mild cognitive impairment asks what lifestyle modification has the best evidence for preventing progression to dementia. Which intervention should be recommended?
questions.explanation: Smoking cessation has strongest evidence for reducing dementia risk and progression.

questions.question_text: An 82-year-old widow develops symptoms of low mood, guilt, and social withdrawal 2 months following the death of her husband. She reports these feelings are slowly improving with support from family and her general practitioner. What is the most likely psychiatric diagnosis according to the conceptual framework in the source?
questions.explanation: Adjustment disorders as common following physical illness and by their nature are transient. While bereavement is not identical to physical illness, the source's description of adjustment disorders as reactive, time-limited conditions with gradual improvement fits this presentation. The key distinguishing feature is the transient nature and clear environmental stressor. Major depressive disorder would typically involve more severe, persistent symptoms. This requires understanding the definition of adjustment disorder from the source material. ---

questions.question_text: Memory preserved in normal aging
questions.explanation: Procedural memory (memory for skills and habits) is preserved in normal aging. Speed of processing, working memory, attention, and executive function typically decline with normal aging.

questions.question_text: Secondary depression may be caused by physical illnesses in elderly people. Which of the following is correct with regard to depression and physical illness?

options.text: main depression is not diagnosed in the presence of chronic medical illnesses in elderly people
Secondary depression is more commonly than main depression in elderly people
Subclinical hypothyroidism is more commonly among depressed than non-depressed elderly people
Depression is two to three times more commonly in those with chronic medical illnesses
Many apparent physical illnesses are found on assessment to be due to somatoform disorders

correct_answer.text: Depression is two to three times more commonly in those with chronic medical illnesses

questions.explanation: Late-life depression often occurs in the context of medical health issues; it is two to three times more common in the medically ill elderly patient. The diagnosis ‘depression due to a general medical condition’ (more commonly, secondary depression) is used when depressed mood or anhedonia occur in patients already diagnosed with an illness that is clearly linked to depression as a physiological consequence. For example, nearly 25% of patients with myocardial infarction have a major depressive episode. Primary depression can exist alongside a general medical condition with no direct physiological relationship. In fact, such co-existing depression and a general medical condition is more common than depression secondary to medical problems. Depression may also exacerbate the outcome of medical illnesses. Although hypothyroidism is considered to cause depression traditionally, recent studies show that a TSH value of 10 μU/L or greater was found in only 0.7% of elderly patients with clinical depression. Thus the rate of subclinical hypothyroidism in an elderly depressed group may be similar to that of the elderly population in general. Kroenke K. A 75-year-old man with depression. Journal of the American Medical Association 2002; 287: 1568–1576.

questions.question_text: In old age, when a person gives up due to socio-economic reasons, which concept applies?
questions.explanation: Downshifting refers to voluntary opting out of a pressurized career and giving up a well-paid job for a more fulfilling life, often due to socio-economic or lifestyle considerations.

questions.question_text: An old man comes with poor sleep and daytime drowsiness, taking more than 20 minutes to get up from sleep after taking diazepam.
questions.explanation: Diazepam has an elimination half-life of 20-50 hours. questions.question_text: Which memory is preserved in normal aging?
questions.explanation: Procedural memory, working memory, and attention are relatively preserved in normal aging, while processing speed and episodic memory typically decline.

questions.question_text: An older female patient in a nursing facility repeatedly urinates in her bed. When she feels the need to urinate, she rings a bell for assistance to ambulate to the bathroom. The staff is taking 2 to 3 minutes to answer the call bell, which does not constitute neglect. A permanent urinary catheter puts the woman at risk of infection.

Development of post-traumatic stress disorder from diagnosis

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is not shown to be linked to an increase in the risk of development of alcohol abuse in elderly people?

options.text: Presence of an organic mental disorder
Presence of a close drinking companion or household member

correct_answer.text: Presence of an organic mental disorder

questions.explanation: Genetic and familial factors probably account for most cases of alcohol problems that begin in adulthood and continue through to older age. Late-onset cases are associated with much lower rates of family alcoholism. Compared with early-onset cases, late-onset problem drinkers also tend to have less psychopathology. In fact, the notion that late-onset alcohol dependence usually occurs secondary to a mood or organic mental disorder has not been upheld in recent systematic studies. The inability to cope with major losses, chronic psychosocial strains, or transient negative affects such as depression or loneliness, are associated with new or renewed problem drinking. The pathophysiological effects of alcohol may be more serious in elderly people because of an age-related increase in biological sensitivity to alcohol and in peak blood level following a standard alcohol load. In addition, alcohol also aggravates many pre-existing diseases that are more common in later life. Gelder MG, et al., eds. New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry. Oxford University Press, 2000, p. 1638.

questions.question_text: At what age is early-onset Alzheimer's disease typically diagnosed?

questions.question_text: When compared with those with late-onset depression, elderly individuals with early-onset depression have

options.text: Less commonly family history of mood disorders
Lower rates of cerebrovascular disease and cognitive decline
Greater increase in size of the lateral ventricles of the brain

questions.explanation: Elderly people with depression may have a relapse or recurrence of a depressive disorder from adulthood (early onset) or they might have fresh onset late-life depression. Late-onset major depression includes a large subgroup of patients with neurological problems. It is possible that milder, unnoticed episodes of depression with early-onset might be a risk factor for late-life depression by contributing to brain abnormalities. When compared with elderly individuals with early-onset major depression, patients with late-onset major depression have a less frequent family history of mood disorders, a higher prevalence of disorders of dementia, a larger impairment in neuropsychological tests, a higher rate of dementia development on follow-up, more neurosensory hearing impairment, a greater enlargement in lateral brain ventricles, and more white matter hyperintensities. Alexopoulos GS. Depression in the elderly. Lancet 2005; 365: 1961–1970.

options.text: Side effects, which may impact the patient's physical health condition
Availability of the drug at the patient's local pharmacy

correct_answer.text: Side effects, which may impact the patient's physical health condition

This reflects the principle that antidepressant selection in older people with comorbid physical illness requires consideration of side effect profiles relative to their physical health. The other options are either not mentioned or are not the primary consideration identified in the source. ---

questions.question_text: An 85-year-old with Alzheimer's - risk increases with age beyond 65 years. By age 85, risk is increased by how many times compared to age 65?
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's risk doubles every 5 years after age 65. From age 65 to 85 is 20 years (4 intervals of 5 years). 2^4 = 16 times increase. At age 65, risk is approximately 5%, and at age 85, approximately 40% - roughly an 8-fold increase in absolute risk.

questions.question_text: Senile self-neglect with signifi cant reclusiveness in elderly people is called Diogenes syndrome. Which of the following is false with respect to this condition?

options.text: Cannot be diagnosed in the absence of cognitive impairment
Family members often bring the person to medical attention
linked to high degree of mortality
Associated with significant social isolation and lack of engagement

correct_answer.text: Cannot be diagnosed in the absence of cognitive impairment

questions.explanation: Patients with so-called Diogenes syndrome are characterized by aloofness and breakdown of self-care to a severe extent; in some cases they may pose an environmental health hazard. Many of them are resistant to intervention from any agency, including relatives. Men and women are equally affected, but the condition is rare. An annual incidence of 0.5 per 1000 of the population aged over 60 years is reported. Diogenes syndrome is not a diagnostic category and patients form a heterogeneous group with respect to diagnoses. Some of them may have personality disorders, some have dementia while some are diagnosed with late-onset schizophrenia. Overall mortality is high for such patients. Murray R, Kendler K, et al., eds. Essential Psychiatry, 4th edn. Cambridge University Press, 2008, p. 374–75.

questions.question_text: Which type of memory is preserved in normal aging?
questions.explanation: In normal aging, procedural memory (motor skills and habits) is generally preserved. Processing speed, attention, and executive function typically decline with age, whereas implicit/procedural learning remains relatively intact.

questions.question_text: A 78-year-old man with vascular dementia is prescribed apixaban for atrial fibrillation. He develops worsening agitation and is started on a new psychotropic medication. Two weeks later, concerns arise about potential thromboembolic complications. Which medication is most likely responsible for reducing apixaban efficacy and increasing DVT risk?
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine induces CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein, reducing apixaban levels and increasing thrombotic risk.

questions.question_text: The strongest treatable risk factor for vascular dementia is;
questions.explanation: The Syst-Eur and PROGRESS studies showed small but significant reductions in dementia from treating hypertension (Forette 2002; Tzourio 2003). Hypertension is now considered as strongest treatable risk factor for vascular dementia.

questions.question_text: A 79-year-old man with a history of progressive cognitive decline for the last year has difficulty in remembering names but is good at day-to-day functioning. The most likely diagnosis is;
questions.explanation: In the early stages of Alzheimer's disease, people often present with cognitive difficulties such as forgetting trivial details, names, faces, etc. but will show largely preserved functional abilities.

questions.question_text: An 81-year-old woman with dementia presented to the hospital with chest pain. Upon admission, she becomes acutely confused and agitated. She is combative and attacks a nurse who tried to pacify her. She refuses to accept a nurse to sit beside her and observe her continuously and threatens to kick anyone who attempts this. The best option available for the medical team is

options.text: Use heavy sedation to prevent physical attacks
Use temporary physical or pharmacological restraints with regular re-evaluation of her
Continue to try verbal de-escalation to calm her down

correct_answer.text: Use temporary physical or pharmacological restraints with regular re-evaluation of her

questions.explanation: Using rapid tranquillisation or physical restraints is sometimes necessary for the elderly to reduce harm to the patient and/or the health professionals. Only a minimal amount of restraint should be used, and the need for continued restraint re-evaluated frequently. Transferring to a psychiatry ward does not seem practical at this time due to the acute level of patient agitation and his behaviors, and verbal de-escalation has already failed to calm the patient. Involving a carer may help to calm the patient down, and that individual may be able to assist in making decisions for his care.

questions.question_text: The most important and common bedside test that is used in demonstrating age-associated memory impairment would be;
questions.explanation: Approximately 40% of individuals aged 65 and over show AAMI. Cognitive testing has demonstrated that  memory for non-verbal material seems to be more affected by aging than memory for verbal material, and delayed recall is more affected than immediate recall. Here the subject is given a list of 20 words and then ask him or her to recall as many as possible in 20 minutes. Finally, the score is compared with standardised scores for the given age.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is an ICD-10 diagnostic feature of frontotemporal dementia?
questions.explanation: The ICD-10 diagnostic features of fronto-temporal dementia include a progressive dementia commencing in late middle life, with slowly progressing changes of character and social deterioration, followed by impairment of intellect, memory and language functions. The behavioural manifestations commonly precede memory impairment.

questions.question_text: A 55-year old man has been suffering from short-term memory problems, and other problems related to concentration. Otherwise, his daily activities are not affected. Which of the following is he most likely to develop?
questions.explanation: Patients with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), if progressing to further deterioration, are most likely to convert to Alzheimer's-like dementia.

questions.question_text: Mrs. Baker is a 78-year-old woman who has recently been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. Her daughter informed her old age psychiatrist that 2 of Mrs. Baker's 4 siblings have also received the same diagnosis. She asks about the possible genetic factors involved in the development of Alzheimer's disease. How many times more likely is a patient to develop Alzheimer's disease if they are a heterozygote for ApoE4?
questions.explanation: ApoE2 is protective against Alzheimer's disease. Most of the population (around 60%) have 'double dose' of the APOE3 gene and therefore are at 'average risk'. An individual is 3 to 4 times more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease if they are heterozygous for ApoE4 (i.e. one copy). Nearly 25% of the population is homozygous. This increases to 10-15 times if they are homozygous (i.e. 2 copies) for ApoE4.
